title: What Is Title Insurance and What California Homebuyers Should Know
content_html:
What Title Insurance Actually Covers

When you buy a home, you're not just purchasing the physical structure and land — you're purchasing legal ownership, or "title," to that property. Title insurance protects against problems with that ownership claim that existed before your purchase but weren't discovered until after closing (or sometimes even years later). This is different from homeowners insurance, which covers future physical damage to the property. Title insurance looks backward, covering issues rooted in the property's history.

Common problems title insurance is designed to address include:

  • A previous owner's unpaid debts or liens that were never properly cleared from public records
  • Errors in prior deeds, wills, or divorce settlements that affected how the property was transferred
  • Forged signatures or fraud somewhere in the chain of ownership
  • Undisclosed heirs who could later claim an ownership interest
  • Clerical or recording errors in the county's public records
  • Boundary or easement disputes that weren't apparent at the time of purchase

If one of these issues surfaces after you own the home, title insurance covers the legal defense costs and, depending on the policy, compensates you for a covered loss — rather than leaving you to fight the claim, or absorb the financial hit, on your own.

How the Title Search Fits In

Before a title insurance policy is issued, a title company conducts a search of public records related to the property — deeds, liens, judgments, tax records, and other recorded documents — to identify anything that could cloud ownership. Most problems get resolved during this search-and-clear process, before you ever close escrow. Title insurance exists for the smaller set of issues that a records search can't catch: fraud, forgery, undisclosed heirs, or clerical errors that simply aren't visible in the public record no matter how carefully it's reviewed.

This title search typically happens during the same window as your other escrow process steps, and any issues the search turns up are usually addressed before closing, as part of clearing title for transfer.

Owner's Policy vs. Lender's Policy

In a typical California home purchase, two separate title insurance policies may come into play:

  • Lender's title policy: If you're financing the purchase, your lender will require a title policy protecting its financial interest in the property up to the loan amount. This protects the lender, not you.
  • Owner's title policy: This is optional but protects your interest as the buyer, typically for the full purchase price, for as long as you or your heirs own the property. It's a one-time premium paid at closing, not an ongoing cost like homeowners insurance.

Because the lender's policy only protects the lender's stake in the loan, buyers who want protection for their own equity need to separately obtain an owner's policy. Which party customarily pays for which policy, and how the cost is split, is something to discuss directly with your escrow or title officer, since practices can vary by transaction and by negotiation between buyer and seller.

Why This Matters in California Specifically

California real estate transactions typically involve an escrow process where a neutral third party — the escrow holder — manages the exchange of funds and documents, and title work is coordinated alongside that process. Because California uses a recording system for property records rather than a title registry, ownership history is established through the chain of recorded documents at the county recorder's office. That system generally works well, but it also means an error, gap, or fraudulent document introduced decades earlier can theoretically resurface. Title insurance is the mechanism that shifts that risk away from the current buyer.

This is worth keeping in mind alongside the other disclosure and inspection steps in a California purchase — title issues are a different category of risk than the physical or environmental disclosures covered in a seller disclosure statement or a natural hazard disclosure. Disclosures address what the seller knows about the property's condition and history; title insurance addresses the legal soundness of the ownership claim itself, independent of what anyone currently involved in the sale actually knows.

What Homebuyers Should Actually Do

A few practical steps can help you understand your title insurance coverage rather than simply signing paperwork at closing:

  • Read the preliminary title report, sometimes called a "prelim," when your escrow or title company provides it. This document lists what the title search found — existing liens, easements, restrictions, or other recorded items affecting the property — before the policy is finalized.
  • Ask what's excluded. Every title policy has exclusions and exceptions, and it's worth understanding what specifically is and isn't covered for your property.
  • Decide about the owner's policy early, since it's typically arranged as part of the same closing process as the lender's policy, and understanding the cost and coverage upfront avoids last-minute decisions during escrow.
  • Ask questions of your escrow or title officer directly. They handle these policies daily and can explain anything on the prelim or the policy itself in plain terms specific to your transaction.

Title insurance is one piece of a larger closing process that also includes purchase agreement contingencies and, for financed buyers, the terms of your loan. Understanding how the pieces fit together — rather than treating title insurance as just another line item on the closing disclosure — helps you close with a clearer picture of what you're actually protected against.
